questions.question: What is the safest first step when Python raises a traceback?
options: Delete the function and start again.
Catch all exceptions with bare `except`.
Ignore it if the code works sometimes.
Read the exception type/message and the failing line in your code.
questions.explanation: The exception type tells you what went wrong and the traceback pinpoints the line; reading both is always faster than guessing, deleting code, or silently swallowing the error.

questions.question: Why is bare `except:` considered risky?
options: It is always a syntax error.
It can hide unexpected bugs and swallow important exceptions.
It only catches ValueError.
It makes code run slower than loops.
questions.explanation: A bare except catches every exception including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, hiding bugs that should surface; catching only the specific exception you expect keeps diagnostic signals visible.

questions.question: Which inputs should tests include beyond happy-path values?
options: Empty, invalid, boundary, zero/negative, and duplicate cases.
Only random large numbers.
Only the exact example shown in docs.
No edge cases if code looks correct.
questions.explanation: Edge cases expose the hidden assumptions that pass silently on normal inputs; empty inputs, boundaries, and invalid values are where most real bugs live.

questions.question: What does `assert x > 0` do?
options: Skips the check in all modes.
Prints whether x is positive.
Raises AssertionError if the condition is false.
Converts x into a positive number.
questions.explanation: assert evaluates the condition and raises AssertionError immediately if it is false; it does not print results or modify the value, making it useful for encoding expectations in tests.

questions.question: When should you raise a new exception?
options: Whenever you want to stop code quickly, regardless of context.
When input/state violates a function contract and caller must know.
Never; always return None.
Only inside class methods.
questions.explanation: Raise an exception with a clear message when a function's contract is violated and the local code cannot recover; returning None silently hides the problem from the caller.

questions.question: Which tool ensures cleanup runs whether or not an exception occurs?
options: finally block (or equivalent context manager cleanup).
continue statement
break statement
assert statement
questions.explanation: A finally block always executes after try/except completes, regardless of whether an exception was raised or caught, making it the right place for resource cleanup like closing files.

questions.question: What is a reliable debugging workflow?
options: Suppress the exception and continue.
Change many lines quickly and rerun once.
Ask the AI for a full rewrite immediately.
Reproduce, inspect, hypothesize, change one thing, retest.
questions.explanation: Changing one thing at a time and retesting isolates the cause; changing many lines at once introduces new variables and makes it impossible to know what actually fixed the problem.

questions.question: What is the best reason to keep tests around after fixing a bug?
options: They force every function to use classes.
They eliminate all need for logging.
They prevent the same bug from silently returning.
They make exceptions unnecessary.
questions.explanation: A regression test encodes the exact scenario that broke before; if future changes re-introduce the bug, the test fails immediately instead of letting it slip back into production.
